svg.title: What happens on the first start after an upgrade
svg.desc: A top-to-bottom flow of the first start after a Continuity upgrade. Step one asks whether the update rewrites records that already exist. If it does, a complete safety copy of the database is written beside it first, and that copy is deleted automatically after three clean starts. If the update only adds things, such as a new table or a new column, no safety copy is taken at all — the branch that surprises people. Both paths then reach step two, where the database format is updated. Step three runs routine cleanup: tool-call records from sessions that finished more than fourteen days ago are deleted, and memory relevance is aged by the clock, while memories themselves are never deleted. A final note explains that deleting records does not shrink the database file, so reclaiming disk space needs a separate manual run of continuity prune.
svg.text: The first start after an upgrade
All of this happens before Continuity answers its first request.
1. Safety copy — taken only sometimes
Does this update rewrite records that already
exist, or does it only add new ones?
adds only
No safety copy is taken at all
Updates that only ADD something —
a new table, a new column — skip the
copy entirely. This one surprises people.
rewrites existing records
Full safety copy taken first
A complete copy of the database is written
beside it. It is deleted automatically after
three clean starts.
2. Database format updated
Both paths arrive here. The update either
completes in full or is rolled back — it
never lands half applied.
3. Routine cleanup runs
Tool-call records are deleted once their
session finished more than 14 days ago.
Memory relevance is aged by the clock.
Memories themselves are never deleted.
Disk space is not returned yet
Deleting records frees space inside the
file, but the file itself stays the same
size on disk.
Run `continuity prune` yourself to
compact it. Nothing does it for you.
Cleanup is not an upgrade step alone — it also runs once a day while Continuity is up.
If a safety copy is required but cannot be written, the upgrade stops rather than proceeding without one.
